newsitem.title: ITALY: BT aims to compete in all Italy phone sectors.
newsitem.headline: BT aims to compete in all Italy phone sectors.

text.p: British Telecom aims to compete with Italy's national phone operator Telecom Italia in the mobile phone, business telephony and even in the domestic phone sector, a senior BT official said.

Pat Gallagher, head of BT's European operations, told the Corriere della Sera newspaper at the weekend that the January 1998 date set for the liberalisation of the European telecoms market would revolutionise the whole sector.

He said BT's alliance with Italian TV media group Mediaset and BNL bank in its Albacom joint venture was set to expand rapidly, first in the cellular phone sector and then to study the prospect of possibly making an offer for the Olivetti -controlled Omnitel GSM operator.
Gallagher said BT's maxi-merger with MCI would not divert BT from its European plans.

"On the contrary, it reinforces us and allows us to create a global force to take on the markets. We're investing in Europe and we've no intention of taking a step backwards," he was quoted as saying.
BT has pinpointed six major European potential markets -- Germany, France, Spain, the Netherlands, Sweden and Italy.
"In Italy, we will compete head to head with Telecom Italia," Gallagher said. "Our aim is to become a complete operator, not only for business, but also for households.
"And we'll do the same in each of the six countries we've chosen in Europe. The ultimate goal is to build a pan-European business," he said.
In Italy, BT had chosen Mediaset and BNL as partners "for political, financial reasons and because we have a common vision."
The three groups were studying whether to compete for a licence to become Italy's third mobile phone operator, after Telecom Italia Mobile (TIM) and Omnitel.
"But if market conditions and regulations at the time of the bid auction were to convince us that a third operator wouldn't make money then we would have to think of an alternative.
"As an alternative hypothesis we are looking at Omnitel, but there's a problem in that the rules of its statute forbids the control of the company changing for five years.
"But it is a possibility that we are studying closely," Gallagher added.
